title: Pot roast
subtitle: Chuck braised low and slow with root vegetables
excerpt: A pot roast is a piece of beef chuck braised in a covered pot with stock, onion, carrot, and celery for 3 to 4 hours until the meat is tender enough to break with a fork. The braising liquid becomes the sauce. It is the defining American Sunday-dinner dish.
sourceNotes: Fannie Farmer, The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book (1896), Project Gutenberg. Pot roast appears as a braised beef method in the original edition. Edna Lewis, The Taste of Country Cooking (1976), gives the Southern pot-roast tradition with root vegetables and pan gravy.

recipe.freezeNotes: The braised meat and vegetables freeze well in the cooking liquid for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight and reheat gently in a covered pot.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the day before and refrigerate in the pot. Reheat covered in a 160°C oven for 45 minutes. The flavour improves overnight.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cooking in a covered pot with a small amount of liquid over low heat for a long time, so the meat becomes tender as the collagen in the connective tissue converts to gelatin.

content.text: A pot roast is beef chuck

in a covered pot with aromatics and stock for the better part of an afternoon until the meat pulls apart and the liquid has concentrated into a rich, dark sauce. Chuck is the right cut: it has enough fat and connective tissue to reward long, slow cooking. A lean joint dries out.
Searing the meat well before adding the liquid is worth doing. It takes ten minutes and adds significant flavour to the finished sauce.

items.prepNote: tied into a compact shape if loose

content.text: Heat the oven to 160°C. Pat the {{beef-chuck}} of beef chuck dry with kitchen paper. Season all over with salt and pepper. Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in the Dutch oven over high heat until smoking. Sear the beef on all sides for about 3 minutes per side until deeply browned all over. Remove and set aside.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the {{onion}} onions, {{carrot}} carrots, and {{celery}} celery to the pot and cook for 4 minutes. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and {{tomato-puree}} of tomato purée. Cook for 1 minute.

Pour in {{stock-beef}} of beef stock and {{tinned-tomatoes}} of chopped tomatoes. Add {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce, the {{thyme}} sprigs of thyme, and the {{bay-leaves}} of bay. Return the beef to the pot. The liquid should come halfway up the meat. Bring to a simmer.

Cover tightly and transfer to the oven. Cook for 2 hours. Add the {{potato}} potatoes around the beef. Re-cover and cook for a further 1 to 1.5 hours until the beef is completely tender and a fork meets no resistance. Rest for 15 minutes before serving.

items.cause: Oven too low, or the cut was different from chuck (a lean joint won't respond the same way).
items.fix: Raise the oven to 170°C and cook for another 30 minutes. Check that the joint is actually chuck or a similar collagen-rich cut.

items.cause: Too much liquid added, or the pot was not covered properly.
items.fix: Remove the meat and vegetables. Boil the sauce on the hob for 10 minutes until reduced. Add a teaspoon of cornflour dissolved in cold water to thicken further.

items.cause: Added too early in the cook.
items.fix: Add waxy potatoes (Charlotte, new potatoes) in the final 1 hour rather than at the start, or use a firmer potato variety.

content.text: Mississippi pot roast swaps the stock and tomatoes for a packet of ranch dressing mix and a jar of pepperoncini, cooked in a slow cooker. Yankee pot roast from New England uses cider vinegar in the braising liquid for a sharper result. Parsnips and turnips work alongside or instead of the carrots.

The pot roast is the American equivalent of the British Sunday joint, a single-pot centrepiece built for a table of six on a cold afternoon. It appears in American cookery from the late nineteenth century and remains one of the most-cooked dishes in the country. The genius is the braising liquid: there is no separate sauce to make.
